content.summary_of_the_paper: The proposed method, Opportunistic Actor-Critic (OPAC) uses the Clipped Triple Q-learning technique for better bias control. Essentially it uses 3 critics and takes the mean of the smallest two Q values for the Q target computation. The authors claim that OPAC combines the strength of TD3 and SAC, and show OPAC outperform them and another competing algorithm TADD in MuJoCo tasks. Additional empirical analysis and theoretical results show that OPAC can lead to better value estimations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
- On the tested MuJoCo tasks, OPAC performs consistently better than SAC/TD3 baselines. 
- Empirical analysis and theoretical results support OPAC can be a better bias control technique compared to clipped double Q. For example, Figure 2 shows OPAC's value estimates are the closest to true value compared to the other methods. Hyperparameter studied which is good. 
- technical details and hyperparameters reported which is good 
- Simplicity: method is overall simple and easy to understand 
- Overall writing and presentation is good

Weaknesses:
- Related work is a bit lacking: How does your method relate to/compare to SOTA bias reduction methods on Gym such as REDQ (Randomized Ensembled Double Q Learning, ICLR 2021) or TQC (Controlling Overestimation Bias with Truncated Mixture of Continuous Distributional Quantile Critics, ICML 2020)? Both these works have far superior performance compared to TD3/SAC which are baselines from a few years ago. And since this work is discussing balancing over/under-estimation bias, another important related work is Maxmin Q-learning: Controlling the Estimation Bias of Q-learning (ICLR 2020). 
- Novelty: considering missing related works that extensively study how ensemble can be used to reduce bias and improve performance, the novelty of the proposed technique seems to be a bit limited. 
- Significance of results: partly due to missed related works, it is unclear how this method compares to the SOTA methods. The other baselines mentioned in the paper are a bit old or not competitive.  
- Some claims are not well supported: In the abstract, I'm not convinced by the argument on how TD3 is better in simpler tasks and SAC in complex tasks. Their differences are quite small, and SAC has a better exploration scheme so it has the same or better performance in all tasks. But TD3 can also be improved by just modify how its exploration actions are generated (Methods like DrQv2 do not use entropy and their exploration is TD3/DDPG-like). So this argument about simple/complex tasks seems wrong. 

Minor issues, typo for example:
- page 7, "the expected error incurred byOPAC, TADD, ..."
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Overall writing and presentation is clear
Quality: Overall quality is OK
Novelty: a bit limited considering bias reduction papers in the past 2 years
Reproducibility: a number of technical details provided for reproducibility, hyperparameters are studied, adding to reliability of results
content.summary_of_the_review: The major concern is lack of discussion on related SOTA techniques on bias reduction. If this paper is submitted 2 years ago it might be a much stronger paper, but considering papers that work on ensemble-based bias reduction and achieve much stronger results on MuJoCo, the novelty and significance of this work seem to be a bit limited. The paper still brings some theoretical results and analysis that can be somewhat interesting, but it is unclear if this will really advance the current state-of-the-art. At its current state, it might be difficult to recommend acceptance of this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a novel off-policy RL method, Opportunistic Actor-Critic (OPAC), that combines the important implementation features in the existing SoTA off-policy methods (SAC & TD3).
In additon to those combinations (maximum entropy framework, automatic entropy adjustment, target network, delayed policy updates, addition of noise), OPAC introduces clipped triple Q-learning that takes the mean of the smallest two q-values. Clipped triple Q-learning could balance the overestimation bias of single Q value and the underestimation bias of clipped double Q-learning. The experimental evaluation shows OPAC improves the performances over SAC, TD3 and TADD.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The empirical evaluations on MuJoCo environments (Figure 3) show solid improvement among SAC, TD3 and TADD.
- OPAC seems to successfully handle the over/underestimation bias and estimate the Q-value better (Figure 2).

### Weaknesses
- There are several missing but important previous works: Recent off-policy methods, TQC [1], REDQ [2] and DroQ [3] provide significantly superior performance over SAC and TD3 with some tricks on target Q-value (distributional/ensemble/update ratio). Also, some relevant work (SUNRISE [4]. EMaQ[5]) works on controlling the estimation bias of Q-value with ensembles. The comparison with open-sourced ones and clarification should be included.
- The correctness of the mathematical proof. See `Clarity` in the next section.


[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04269

[2] https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.05982

[3] https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.02034

[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.04938

[5] https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.11091
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Quality
- The formal definition of $\text{mst}(\cdot)$ operator seems missing. Since $\text{mst}(\cdot)$ operator often appears in this paper, the mathematical expression would help.
- It's better to unify the style in Algorithm 1: the sampled action of the 1st line in the for-loop is different from that of the 4th line. It can cause a misunderstanding of $+\eta$.

### Clarity
There are some unclear points in the paper:
- In Section 6, the target Q values are computed with action $\pi(s')$, while in Section 7, the action distribution of the policy $\pi(a'|s')$ appears in the same equation (e.g. equation 11). I think the former notation is often used for deterministic policy, but I guess OPAC uses a stochastic policy like SAC. 
- Since $\sigma_{\theta}(s)$ is a $|\mathcal{A}|$-dimensional vector, the expectation of equation 13 and related ones are not scalar values. The related proof seems to ignore the dimensionality of the policy. Also, the diagonal covariate matrix is implicitly assumed.
- it might better clearly state that the expected error is better when it is near to zero (related to Figure 1 and Section 6). The author said like "$Z$ is expected error, $Z_{min} < Z_{mst}$,  so $\text{mst}$ is better than $\text{min}$". Without any assumption, that might cause misunderstanding (we usually think that a smaller error is better).

### Originality
The proposed methods OPAC largely depend on the implementation details in SAC and TD3, and, as far as I checked the ablation,  clipped triple Q-learning are also co-dependent to those. The one interesting but missing ablation is M=2 version of OPAC, i.e. for the target value, take the mean of two q-values, instead of the smallest (Clipped double Q) or the mean of the smallest two (Clipped triple Q). Guessing from Figure 1 (b), that might outperform M=3.
content.summary_of_the_review: While OPAC shows improved performance over SAC and TD3 with the combined techniques and clipped triple Q-learning, clipped triple Q-learning also seems to be co-dependent on those existing techniques (delayed update/noise/max-ent, etc). In addition, the discussion on the recent SoTA off-policy methods is lacking, and there is minor (but in many part) flaw in the mathematical proof. Considering those aspects, I vote for rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper propose a method to tackle the underestimation bias problem of TD3 and SAC. A Clipped Triple Q-learning method that takes the mean of the smallest two Q-values is proposed. This paper propose the OPAC method combining TD3, SAC and the Clipped Triple Q-learning. Experimental results on several MuJoCo environments validate its effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1.Overestimation and underestimation are important topics for deep reinforcement learning.

2.The paper is well written and easy to follow.

3.The paper provides detailed specifications about experimental setup and evaluations.

Weakness:

1.The paper claim that it can reduce the overestimation bias compared with TD3. SD3(NIPS 2020), DATD3(AAAI 2022) also can reduce the underestimation bias of TD3. However, the paper does not compare these methods in terms of both estimation bias and performance.

2.The novelty of the paper is limited as some parts seems like a direct combination of TD3 and SAC, but the paper does not provide detailed insight of why SAC works in complex envs while TD3 works in simple envs.

3.Theorem 2 assumes that Yi follows a uniform distribution, which might be too strong in practice.

4.The experimental results are not quite convincing. TD3 fails to learn in Humanoid-v2, can you explain the reason?

2.The novelty of this paper is limited, and some baselines are missing.

3.The paper provides the code of implementations.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a version of Clipped Double Q-Learning (CDQ)  [1]. CDQ involves training an ensemble of two critics and taking a minimum of them for computing TD-targets, while the method proposed in this work fits three critics and takes a mean of two smallest values.

[1] Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods
Scott Fujimoto, Herke van Hoof, David Meger
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
Addressing the underestimation problem of CDQ is an interesting and valuable problem for the deep learning community.

# Weaknesses
* The novelty of the approach is limited. Even though taking a mean of the two smallest values has not been done in prior work, alternative ways to extend the ensemble have already been studied in REDQ [1]. Moreover, the paper is missing crucial comparisons to [1]. In particular, it's essential to see how this works compares to a version of REDQ with three critics. 
* The experimental comparison is flawed. The results reported in SACv2 [2] are better than SAC results reported in this work and match OPAC.


## Minor comments
* The abstract and introductions mention that this approach combines the best properties of TD3 and SAC. However, the combination of tricks from the algorithms is not ablated in the paper. The authors propose to add noise to a'; however, SAC already samples actions with Gaussian noise. Do you add additional noise on top of the Gaussian noise?

[1] Randomized Ensembled Double Q-Learning: Learning Fast Without a Model
Xinyue Chen, Che Wang, Zijian Zhou, Keith Ross
[2] Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. However, the novelty is limited. The paper misses comparisons to important prior work (see above).
content.summary_of_the_review: Even though the paper explores an interesting direction, I cannot recommend it for acceptance at ICLR. It misses comparisons to important prior work, and the experimental evaluation exhibits significant flaws.

content.title: Opportunistic Actor-Critic (OPAC) with Clipped Triple Q-learning
content.TL;DR: OPAC achieves higher average rewards than relevant baselines and mitigates the underestimation bias with the help of Clipped Triple Q-learning.
content.abstract: Despite being the most successful model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms in recent years, Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) have their respective downsides--TD3 performs well in simple tasks, while SAC does so in relatively complicated ones. However, they also suffer from underestimation due to Clipped Double Q-learning, i.e., taking a minimum of two Q-values. This paper introduces Opportunistic Actor-Critic (OPAC), an ensemble model-free deep RL algorithm that performs well in simple and complex tasks. OPAC combines the features of TD3 and SAC under one roof to retain their respective benefits. It also employs three critics and considers taking the mean of the smallest two Q-values for updating the shared target, dubbed Clipped Triple Q-learning. Our analytical results establish that Clipped Triple Q-learning incurs less underestimation than Clipped Double Q-learning. Furthermore, we have systematically evaluated OPAC in MuJoCo environments, and the empirical results indicate that OPAC attains higher average rewards than the current baselines.
